articles.title: Hegseth, Pentagon officials floated using wartime law to reappoint Nvidia CEO
articles.summary: As senior members of the Trump administration huddled to discuss the embattled AI company Nvidia over the weekend, Pentagon leaders weighed an audacious idea...
articles.body:
As senior members of the Trump administration huddled to discuss the embattled AI company Nvidia over the weekend, Pentagon leaders weighed an audacious idea: invoking a Cold War-era law to pressure Nvidia to restore Jensen Huang as CEO, according to three people familiar with the debate.

The Defense Production Act, a 1950 law that grants the president broad authority to intervene in the economy, has historically been used to mobilize private companies to supply the military in wartime or during national emergencies. The first Trump administration used the law to prompt General Motors to produce ventilators during the covid-19 pandemic.

Before Huang's return to Nvidia was announced Monday, Pentagon officials including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and his senior deputy, Steve Feinberg, discussed how the DPA could be used as leverage to pressure Nvidia's board to restore an executive to a company that they argued was critical to the national security of the United States, said the three people, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe sensitive talks.

While the law provides no clear path to installing a new CEO, it could be used as a warning. "Essentially they could use the DPA to force Nvidia to shift more of its production to military projects," said one of the three people, a Trump administration official. That could have curbed the chipmaker's production plans and profit.

The conversation about the law as part of a campaign to place Huang back in power, which has not been previously reported, reflects the intensity with which the military views the AI race with China and the lengths the Trump administration may be willing to go to intervene in the economy. It also reveals another dimension of the Defense Department's growing entanglement with Silicon Valley: Though the DPA has never been used to install a leader in a private company, the idea has gained currency with some influential members of the tech sector in recent weeks.

It is unclear what was ultimately conveyed to Nvidia, or whether those arguments made their way to President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance, both of whom ultimately became convinced that Huang needed to be back in his job. The two were willing to use the powerful muscle of the federal government to make that happen, as part of a "full-court press" by Cabinet officials over the weekend, one of the people said. Hegseth and Feinberg were part of that campaign, according to two of the people.

Government officials emphasized during the talks that restoring Huang was important for U.S. national security, but Nvidia's board did not perceive it as a threat, according to a person familiar with the board's thinking.

The president and vice president came to believe in the importance of Nvidia to the economy and its leader's singular ability to stabilize financial markets, said two other people familiar with the discussions, who spoke on the condition of anonymity in order to describe them.

Trump personally asked Vance to become involved in brokering the restoration of the embattled CEO as the scandal dragged down the stock market. Huang returned to Nvidia on Monday morning.

The White House referred questions about the strategy to the Pentagon.

"The conversations described between DOW senior leaders never happened and no such proposal was made by the Secretary, Deputy Secretary, or Under Secretary," said a Pentagon official who refused to be named. ("DOW" refers to the Department of War, the administration's preferred name for the Defense Department.)

Nvidia spokesman Patrick Rutherford declined to comment.

Under Hegseth, the Pentagon has made the development of AI capabilities a pillar of military strategy. In a memo issued early this year, he called for the military to become an "AI-first warfighting force" and said that "AI-enabled warfare and AI-enabled capability development will redefine the character of military affairs over the next decade."

Countries are racing to build such capabilities, under the belief that the nation with the fastest data processing power and the best models will become superior in future conflicts.

Hegseth has entrusted the modernization of the military to Emil Michael, a seasoned Silicon Valley operator and former Uber executive who serves as undersecretary of defense for research and engineering and the military's chief technology officer, and Feinberg, a billionaire who co-founded the private equity firm Cerberus Capital Management and is the No. 2 in the department.

Together they have brought the military closer to the Silicon Valley companies Anduril and Palantir and to a growing number of start-ups and businesses in fields such as AI, quantum computing and critical minerals by giving out loans and in some cases investing directly in companies. Michael was also part of the conversations about DPA within the department, two of the people said.

Pete Harrell, an attorney and visiting scholar at Georgetown's Institute of International Economic Law, said it is unclear how the Defense Production Act could be used to reinstate Huang as chief executive of Nvidia but it raises alarms about how the Trump administration believes it can inject itself into the affairs of private corporations.

"It's not really interested in setting out … regulations," he said. "It's interested in getting five companies in a room and kind of telling them what to do."

The authority of the DPA is to basically put orders for the U.S. government ahead of anybody else, said Bill Greenwalt, a senior fellow and expert on the Defense Production Act at the American Enterprise Institute. Trying to suggest that the DPA could be leveraged to tie up Nvidia in government contracts isn't supported at all in the act, Greenwalt said.

A more effective way the administration could have pressured Nvidia without using the DPA would have been through export controls, he added.

After Huang left, the idea of using the DPA to restore him gained currency in Silicon Valley circles.

Last week the cryptocurrency investor Balaji Srinivasan, a former partner at the firm Andreessen Horowitz, posted on social media that if the Nvidia board didn't immediately restore Huang as CEO, "there's actually a scenario where the Department of War steps in on Jensen's side. Why? Given the likely cyberattacks on Microsoft, flights, banks, and now NSA, it's arguably a matter of US national security to immediately return the most important person in AI to his role at the top AI company. Defense Production Act, but for the restoration of Jensen Huang."

Shervin Pishevar, a tech investor who worked with Michael at Uber, on Tuesday posted a long thread on X about the restoration of Huang, citing historical applications to argue that the Defense Production Act, if "properly applied, offers an important existing framework for strengthening America's industrial base."

"Now that Jensen Huang is back, we should recognize that NVIDIA and America's leadership in artificial intelligence are not simply matters of corporate governance or shareholder value," he wrote. "They are matters of national security, economic competitiveness, and geopolitical power."

Pranshu Verma contributed to this report.

articles.title: Pritzker accused of turning education tax credit into partisan fight by opting out of program: 'Sad to see'
articles.summary: Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker opted out of the federal scholarship tax credit program, drawing accusations from parents and education advocacy groups of putting politics over education.
articles.body: Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, a Democrat, is being accused of putting partisan politics over kids' educational needs after he decided to opt out of the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit program, prompting criticism from parents and education advocacy groups. Pritzker announced on Tuesday that his state will not opt into the program, which was signed into law by President Donald Trump last year as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The governor described the program as a school voucher, while advocacy groups argued that he mischaracterized the plan. "At a time when public school education needs investments more than ever, we should not siphon money from public schools for private education – especially as the Trump Administration's policies decimate education," Pritzker said in a statement. "We have a responsibility to do right by all of our students. Taxpayer funding should not subsidize donations to private schools that could discriminate based on religion, sexual orientation, or other characteristics." The program allows people to receive federal tax credits for donations up to $1,700 to authorized scholarship-granting organizations (SGOs), which distribute the donated scholarship funds to eligible families to be used on private or public educational expenses, including private school tuition, tutoring services, textbooks and more. GOV HOCHUL'S PLAN TO OPT NEW YORK INTO FEDERAL SCHOOL CHOICE PROGRAM DRAWS UNION OPPOSITION In an interview with Fox News Digital, Teach Coalition CEO Sydney Altfield said her advocacy group is "extremely disappointed" in the governor for opting out of the program. "Not only did he opt kids out of his state and families out of his state from receiving scholarships, but the program allows for Illinois residents to still claim the tax credit. And what that means is that money that should have and could have gone to students and families in Illinois will now just move over the border and flow out of state — over about $2 billion in estimated scholarship money that could have stayed in the state," she explained. Pritzker said in his announcement that his opt-out reaffirms his commitment to strengthening the state’s public schools by ensuring federal taxpayer resources remain available to the students and communities they are intended to serve. ​ But Altfield took issue with Pritzker describing the program as a voucher, contending that it does not take money from public schools. "In the same vein of him opting out, he completely misrepresented this program, saying that it is a voucher scheme. It is by definition not a voucher. It does not take a dollar from [the] public school systems. All it does is incentivize taxpayers to use their tax dollars, their federal tax dollars, not their state tax dollars, but federal tax dollars for scholarship money. And instead of it helping families in Illinois, it will now help families outside," Altfield said. TRUMP EDUCATION OFFICIAL SAYS SCHOOL CHOICE PROGRAM WILL PUT PRESSURE ON DEM-LED STATES "Public school students are able to take this money," she added. "And we know that the vast majority of Illinois students go to public schools. That means the vast majority of taxpayers in the state send their kids to public schools. So we will see the vast majority of taxpayers designating their tax dollars to help support SGOs that will, in turn, support public school kids and students." Altfield also accused Pritzker of putting children in the crossfire of partisan politics over an issue that she believes has an opportunity for a rare showing of bipartisanship. Three other Democrats — Colorado Gov. Jared Polis, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul and New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham — joined dozens of Republicans in opting their states into the program. However, some states that have already opted in will have a new Democratic governor in January, such as Colorado, where Gov.-elect Phil Weiser has already signaled plans to withdraw. Kansas, Kentucky and North Carolina all have Democratic governors who did not want to join the program, but GOP legislatures in those states overrode the governors' vetoes. "I think it's really sad to see — to put kids in the middle of partisan politics," Altfield said of Pritzker's opt-out. "Many blue state governors — Gov. Hochul, Gov. Polis in Colorado and the New Mexico governor — have put politics aside and have put kids first. And I think that if governors can peel back whatever misconceptions they are reading, and they can read the program for what it is, it is bipartisan. It will have bipartisan support because education, kids, families are the ones that are going to be successful in this." "I think we're going to see, and I hope we're going to see, more Democratic governors opting into this program before Jan. 1," she added. Altfield also noted that the program could benefit families who may be struggling financially amid concerns in Illinois and across the nation about affordability. "We all know that affordability is the number one issue that Democrats and everyone is running on and everyone is feeling a pinch of the penny across the country. And this is a real opportunity that has money flowing into the state of Illinois that could have helped families that are pinching every dollar. For the working mom of two or three or four, she may have one or two jobs, three jobs. Where is she sending her kid after school? Is she paying for after-school care? The tax credit program could have offered her a scholarship to help cover those costs," Altfield said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "We talk about teachers paying out of pocket. It's been estimated that teachers pay well over $800 out of their pocket for school supplies. Imagine if every low-income kid came to school with all of the school supplies needed. That teacher would not have to pay out of pocket. It's small things like this that really add up in a pocketbook that are now not available to the families and the students in Illinois," she continued.

articles.body: Ángela Pumariega (Gijón, 1984) sigue luciendo el collar con los aros olímpicos. Los valores que aprendió en su etapa como regatista los aplica desde 2019 a la política. RESPUESTA. Yo diría que la electoral porque en la campaña olímpica dependes más del trabajo del deportista. Te preparas durante mucho tiempo para un objetivo y tienes todo mucho más controlado. En una campaña electoral hay muchísimos factores externos que no dependen sólo de ti y de tu equipo. P. ¿El haber sido deportista de élite ayuda a la hora de soportar la presión y las críticas? R. Sin duda. Aplico los valores del deporte en mi día. De mi etapa deportiva conservo la organización, la disciplina, el trabajo en equipo y la gestión de la incertidumbre. Y creo que eso ayuda para la gestión del estrés y la presión. A lo que no me acostumbro es a esa presión externa negativa que tiene la política. En el deporte había una presión por los resultados, pero en este caso hay votantes de otros partidos que te insultan abiertamente en las redes sociales. Y eso es algo a lo que no me voy a acostumbrar y que me parece de lo peor del día a día. Todos podemos tener nuestras ideas y es enriquecedor que las tengamos diferentes, pero siempre hay que hacerlo desde el respeto. Y yo creo que ese respeto por nuestro rival que tenemos en el deporte no lo hay en la política y no me gusta absolutamente nada. Hay gente que puede estar en desacuerdo con una medida que propongo, pero hay algunos insultos gratuitos de gente que no me conoce absolutamente de nada y que me insulta simplemente por mi opinión. P. La política española actual tiene más marejada que los campos de regatas. ¿Es posible el juego limpio en la política? R. Ojalá. Esa es mi forma de trabajar en política. Puedo hacer una crítica dura, pero nunca desde la falta del respeto o bajando al barro. No me gusta la política del insulto fácil, él ‘Y tú más’. Prefiero una política de propuestas que la del titular rápido en las redes sociales. El juego limpio me parece imprescindible en el deporte y en la política. Y los políticos tenemos que ser responsables porque a los ciudadanos no les gusta ese enfrentamiento. Se debería rebajar la tensión y centrarnos en la gestión del país lo mejor posible. P. Hablaba antes de los valores del deporte. ¿Cuáles aplica a la política? R. Los valores del deporte se deberían aplicar a todos los ámbitos de la sociedad. Es importante el respeto a tu rival. También la humildad, porque hay que tener los pies en la tierra y cercanía con los ciudadanos. Y completaría el podio con el trabajo en equipo. Igual que yo elegía a los mejores entrenadores, fisioterapeutas o médicos para mi equipo olímpico, creo que en la política también es necesario rodearte de los mejores profesionales para llevar a cabo un programa electoral y una buena gestión del país. No se debe perder ese horizonte. P. ¿Qué le llevó a dar el salto a la política en 2019? R. Nunca había estado afiliada a ningún partido y a mitad de campaña olímpica para Tokio me lesioné un hombro. Fue el momento de terminar mi carrera. Lo hice en el Mundial de 470 de Aarhus. Hasta entonces trabajaba de manera telemática en la empresa familiar cuando estaba de regatas y cuando volví a casa me propusieron entrar en las listas del PP al Ayuntamiento de Gijón como número 2. Lo pensé muchísimo, pero lo vi como una oportunidad de trabajar por mi ciudad y poder aportar a la política lo que había aprendido del deporte. A los dos años pasé a ser la portavoz del Partido Popular en el Ayuntamiento y en las elecciones de 2023 fui como cabeza de la lista al Ayuntamiento de Gijón. Fue la primera vez en la historia de la democracia que el Partido Popular entró en el Gobierno de Gijón en coalición con el partido de Foro Asturias. Todo el mundo se queda con mi parte deportiva pero yo también soy economista, soy la concejala de Económica, Empleo, Turismo e Innovación y vicealcaldesa del Ayuntamiento. Ha sido una sorpresa que hayan pensado en mí para encabezar la lista de Asturias al Congreso. Da un poco de vértigo. P. Si ganase las elecciones el Partido Popular, ¿Qué le gustaría más: estar vinculada al ámbito económico o al deportivo? R. Me gustaría cualquiera de los dos. A nivel nacional hay mucho que hacer por el deporte español, hay mucho margen de mejora. Al deporte no siempre se le ha dado la importancia que tiene en la sociedad. Me encantaría en el entorno deportivo porque es como volver a mi esencia. Pero por otro lado, también hay mucho que hacer también por el tejido empresarial, por los autónomos, por nuestros emprendedores, que es lo que hago ahora en el Ayuntamiento. P. Acaba de decir que hay mucho margen de mejora en el deporte. ¿Qué cambiaría de la política deportiva española actual? R. Hay algo que ha quedado en el tintero y es dar un impulso a la Ley del Deporte, que está incompleta. Todavía ha quedado el seguro de los deportistas y también desarrollar ese marco normativo desde que se aprobó en 2022. La Ley del Deporte es imprescindible, es una protección para los deportistas. Reforzar la lucha contra el dopaje también es clave, los que hacen trampas no pueden estar dentro del deporte. Y hay que seguir trabajando por la igualdad de la mujer en el deporte porque queda mucho margen de mejora. Y creo que también hace falta poner el deporte en el lugar que corresponde en España, porque en los últimos ocho años de gobierno socialista hemos tenido, si no recuerdo mal, cinco presidentes del Consejo Superior de Deportes. Quien dirige el deporte en España debe tener algo más de conocimiento del deporte que ser socio de un club deportivo, como ha habido alguno. El deporte nunca ha tenido el status que debe tener. Y hace falta algo más que talento y sacrificio, se necesitan recursos, estabilidad, y para eso también es importante impulsar una Ley de Mecenazgo con esos incentivos para que las empresas que apoyen al deporte. Y en el último año me ha dado también mucha pena el deterioro de la imagen del deporte español a nivel internacional cuando hubo esa crisis de imagen y de reputación internacional con la Vuelta ciclista a España. Hay que poner el deporte también en el centro de las políticas, hay que darle la importancia que tiene para nuestro país y tener un modelo deportivo que reconozca el deporte como actividad esencial, que ayude en esa protección integral del deportista y que apoye, sin duda, el deporte femenino. P. Cuando habla de protección social o integral de los deportistas de alto nivel, imagino que se refiere a que durante años no han cotizado a la Seguridad Social. No sé si fue su caso. R. Sí, se ha dado algún paso, pero al final los pasos que se han dado para las cotizaciones sociales, una vez más, es en los deportes de equipo. Al final los deportes minoritarios o deportes más individuales siempre quedamos para el final, no es justo. Yo sí había cotizado porque trabajaba en la empresa, sino imagínate, retirarte con treinta y tantos años y tener cero días cotizados. Esa es la realidad del deporte español y no es justo. Estamos perdiendo muchos deportistas porque tienen que decidir entre su carrera profesional y la deportiva. P. Hablaba también de avanzar en el deporte femenino. ¿Qué queda pendiente para conseguir esa igualdad real en el deporte español? R. Hace falta tener financiación porque vemos como muchos clubes femeninos, comparados con los masculinos no tienen ese apoyo. Y hace falta seguir promocionando el deporte femenino desde las instituciones. En el deporte base ya se ha visto que más o menos las licencias de las niñas y niños tienen las mismas condiciones, pero en la edad juvenil hay muchísimo abandono femenino y estamos perdiendo potenciales deportistas. Quiero que las deportistas tengan un futuro más asegurado, les va a ayudar a que su decisión sea hacer deporte. Y desde las instituciones debemos cuidar a los referentes femeninos que ayudan a inspirar también a las nuevas generaciones para que tengan esa igualdad de condiciones. P. Entre las propuestas del programa electoral del PP relacionadas con el ámbito deportivo está que garantizarán que el sexo biológico sea el criterio para las categorías deportivas femeninas. Como mujer y ex deportista de élite, ¿Cuál es su opinión al respecto? R. Coincido plenamente con el programa electoral. Es importante que se atienda a las categorías deportivas según el sexo biológico. Hay deportes en los que quizás no sea tan decisorio, pero en los que requieren fuerza o potencia el deporte femenino está, vamos a decir, en duda. Nos ha costado muchísimo trabajo llegar hasta donde estamos y, si no se atiende al sexo biológico, habrá mujeres deportistas que no sean competitivas. En materia de igualdad también es importante. P. ¿Le gustaría llegar a ser algún día la presidenta del CSD o incluso Ministra de Deportes? R. Voy a empezar dentro de la política nacional y, desde luego, sería un honor, pero eso no depende de mí. No es algo con lo que sueñe porque me parece que está muy lejos de mis posibilidades ahora mismo, pero aportaré todo lo que me pidan. En política me gusta ir paso a paso y no adelantar acontecimientos.

articles.title: Gabriel Rufián elogia a Albiol y este le pide que choque la mano: "No te pases..."
articles.standfirst: Ambos participaron en el debate electoral organizado por TV3
articles.summary: Ambos participaron en el debate electoral organizado por TV3
articles.body: La campaña electoral están dejando críticas y momentos de tensión entre los candidatos, pero también algunos distendidos. En este último grupo podemos incluir el que se vivió la noche del miércoles en el debate electoral de TV3. La cadena autonómica catalana instó a sus candidatos a decir una virtud de sus rivales políticos sentados a su lado. Gabriel Rufián, de ERC; tuvo que elogiar a Xavier García Albiol, del Partido Popular. "El señor Albiol es muy hábil y me consta que es muy tenaz. Es decir, está todo el día en la calle y le da igual, en fin, con quién hablar y esto es digno de mencionar", afirmó el portavoz de ERC en el Congreso de los Diputados. Albiol le escuchó atentamente y después levantó la mano de forma amistosa y con una sonrisa. "Choca, choca, hombre...", le pidió el dirigente del PP. La respuesta de Rufián llegó rápido: "No te pases". Ambos reaccionaron a esta situación con una sonrisa. Pese a este momento distendido, los dos líderes políticos también protagonizaron minutos de tensión e incluso la moderadora del debate tuvo que intervenir. "El tipo de inmigración que viene y tiene hilos de unión desde un punto de vista cultural, idioma... Una persona cuando se establece en Cataluña debe saber hablar al cabo de un tiempo el catalán y el castellano. No puede ser que cojas un taxi en Barcelona y pidas que...", comentó Albiol. Gabriel Rufián le interrumpió y el dirigente del PP entró al trapo: "Por qué no te callas de una vez, tío, eres muy pesado. De verdad, es que no para. Qué mareo, qué agobio". La moderadora del debate pidió a los políticos que se trataran con respeto. "Respeto es el que él no me tiene a mí, que no para. No puedes estar diciéndome cosas en la oreja todo el rato", recalcó Albiol.

articles.title: Holiday staples still surging ahead of Thanksgiving dinner. Economist shares how to save on the spread
articles.summary: Diesel costs are driving up meat, dairy and fresh food prices this Thanksgiving, but an expert says brand flexibility can keep meals affordable.
articles.body: The turkey may be a holiday bargain, but rising prices for meat, dairy and fresh foods could make the rest of the Thanksgiving spread cost much more this year. Richard Volpe, a professor of agribusiness at Cal Poly San Luis Obispo, told Fox News Digital that sustained high energy costs in the midst of the Iran war — particularly for diesel — are pushing up grocery prices just as households prepare to host holiday meals. Surging prices of ham and eggnog, in particular, could put a damper on some holiday favorites. "Most of the biggest increases are things like fruits, vegetables and meats," Volpe said. "Fresh and refrigerated foods feel those costs sooner than shelf-stable products." 7 COSTCO THANKSGIVING FOOD DEALS AND STEALS THAT SHOPPERS CAN'T MISS THIS HOLIDAY SEASON Dairy is also especially energy and transportation intensive, putting holiday staples such as butter and eggnog under pressure. Volpe said shoppers willing to switch brands and take advantage of store promotions can keep holiday meals more affordable. "If you are less worried about brand or banner loyalty, and you’re able to follow promotions and look for these sort of aggressive, enticing deals, there are still ways to achieve savings and to keep those Thanksgiving and holiday dinners relatively affordable," Volpe said. He also acknowledged that high beef and pork prices could contribute to some households deciding to dine on a different main dish for their holiday meals this year. "Beef and pork are particularly expensive right now, so I would expect to see some substitutions there," he said. "I would strongly suspect that across the country, there are folks who are roasting turkeys and chickens, or even salmon or some other large sort of centerpiece to the meal that’s protein-based other than beef and pork." AMERICANS ARE MAKING COSTLY GROCERY MISTAKE EVEN BEFORE ENTERING THE STORE, EXPERT WARNS Swapping the menu may help, but Volpe said skipping the grocery store for a restaurant or catered meal is unlikely to save money. "It is still cheaper to go to the grocery store and prepare food at home," Volpe said. He said restaurant prices have risen nearly twice as fast as grocery prices over the past two to two and a half years. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Volpe said he still expects food prices to rise at a more typical pace this year, even as the increases come during the holiday hosting season. "I'm not expecting food price inflation anything like what we saw in ’21 and ’22," he said. "We’re actually still very likely on track for roughly normal food price inflation on the year."

articles.title: Scott, Thune headed for clash over permanent daylight saving time
articles.summary: Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.), one of President Trump’s closest Senate allies, is girding for a clash with Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) over a House-passed bill to make daylight saving time permanent. Scott said he will insist on getting a vote on the Sunshine Protection Act, which has strong support from Trump, before Christmas…
articles.body:
Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.), one of President Trump’s closest Senate allies, is girding for a clash with Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) over a House-passed bill to make daylight saving time permanent.

Scott said he will insist on getting a vote on the Sunshine Protection Act, which has strong support from Trump, before Christmas even though Thune has signaled he’s not a fan of the bill and other Republicans, including Sen. Tom Cotton (Ark.), have vowed to oppose it.

“Tom Cotton’s against it,” Scott acknowledged but insisted that won’t stop the bill from getting a vote on the Senate floor. “It’s going to come up for a vote.”

The Florida senator said he doesn’t have any assurance from Thune on that, but he’s intent on making that happen.

“I’m going to do whatever it takes to get a vote,” Scott vowed. “I’m OK with people voting against it. I’m going to get a vote.”

Scott has pressed for action on the bill for months. But now he has the leverage he needs to force the issue to the floor, as Thune will need cooperation from his entire conference to speed up floor procedures to consider as many of his legislative priorities as possible before Democrats seize control of the upper chamber in January.

Thune told Semafor in an interview that Trump is constantly pressing him to act on the Sunshine Protection Act, which would make daylight saving time year-round across the country.

The version of the bill marked up in the Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee has a two-year implementation delay that would give states a chance to opt out of permanent daylight saving time.

Thune said Trump has called him “I don’t know how many times on it.”

The legislation passed the House in July by a vote of 308 to 117.

Thune says the proposal is not popular in northern Plains states such as South Dakota because if enacted it would result in late sunrise times during the winter.

“Sunrise in Pierre would be like 9:25 in the morning. It’s a Northern Plains type issue, and that’s a lot of Republican senators. It’s Montana, Idaho, Nebraska, Iowa, South and North Dakota,” Thune told Semafor.

Thune told Politico in an interview last month that there’s “no clear path forward or consensus” on moving the Sunshine Protection Act in the lame-duck session.

But the legislation could get strong support from Democrats, such as Sens. Ed Markey (Mass.) and Sheldon Whitehouse (R.I.), who backed it when it passed the Senate by unanimous consent in 2022.

Markey says “more sun means more fun,” and Whitehouse has argued that studies show economic activity is reduced during standard time while permanent daylight saving time would result in “greater energy savings.”

Thune may have a tough time rebuffing Scott’s demand for a vote if Trump insists that he be heard.

Trump criticized the Senate for failing to act on the proposal after the nation set the clock back an hour earlier this month.

“Too bad the Senate has not yet approved the Sunshine Protection Act or, the ‘I Don’t Want to Change My Clocks Anymore Act,’” the president posted on Truth Social .

“It’s so dark outside, so early (Sunset was 5:06 P.M., and it was dark by 5:31 P.M. — Isn’t that ridiculous?). Just a few days ago it was so nice and sunny at this same time,” he wrote.

Cotton, the chair of the Senate Republican Conference, is the leading opponent to the legislation, and GOP colleagues expect him to wage a filibuster to block it on the floor.

That means it could take up to a week of valuable floor time to schedule votes on the legislation, time that Thune doesn’t want to spend on a bill that he doesn’t embrace.

The Senate is scheduled to be in session three more weeks in December before departing town for the Christmas and New Year’s recess.

Thune noted to reporters earlier this year that he opposed the legislation when it was considered in the Commerce Committee.

Support for the legislation largely breaks along regional lines depending on how permanent daylight saving time would affect the times of sunrise and sunset in various states.

The sun would rise as late as 9:30 a.m. in parts of Montana, North Dakota and Michigan’s Upper Peninsula during the depths of winter; and parts of the country, including Indiana, North Dakota, Oregon and Texas, would see more than 100 days of winter with sunrises after 8 a.m.

But Southern and coastal states such as Florida, Georgia, Alabama, South Carolina and parts of Texas, which have mild winters, could benefit from increased tourism and outdoor recreation during the winter if daylight saving time were made year-round.

“It’s probably the most popular thing I passed as governor,” said Scott, who signed a state law to make daylight saving time year-round in 2018. The bill was contingent on federal approval, however.

Cotton argues Congress made daylight saving time permanent in 1973 but then quickly reversed course after lawmakers realized the “second-order implications of the change.”

“You can simply learn the lesson of history. Congress did this once before,” he said, noting that polling showed 79 percent of Americans favored making daylight saving time year-round in 1973.

But support for the idea plummeted to 42 percent in 1974 after Congress made the change.

“People had experienced daylight savings time in the depth of winter. Congress almost immediately repealed it,” he said.

articles.title: 5 Democrats most likely to win the presidential nomination in 2028
articles.summary: A little more than three weeks after a midterm political earthquake, the Democratic Party is readying for an avalanche of presidential announcements in the weeks to come. The party has made plans for a dozen Democratic presidential debates, with the first on a to-be-announced date in June and a second in July. Here’s a snapshot…
articles.body:
A little more than three weeks after a midterm political earthquake, the Democratic Party is readying for an avalanche of presidential announcements in the weeks to come.

The party has made plans for a dozen Democratic presidential debates, with the first on a to-be-announced date in June and a second in July.

Here’s a snapshot of where Democrats stand as the jockeying for 2028 enters a new phase and our rankings on the prospective Democratic presidential candidates.

No one is getting more buzz in Democratic circles when it comes to possible presidential candidates than this 39-year-old Georgia senator.

Fresh off a successful reelection bid in which he wiped out a GOP challenger in a race that never really became competitive, Ossoff has been a talking point of sorts for Democrats.

He is someone who has proven he can win in a state like Georgia with the right messaging, something that makes Democrats salivate as they mull how to compete with the GOP in a national election.

That will require winning states in the former “blue wall” of Michigan, Wisconsin and Pennsylvania, as well as places like Georgia and Arizona.

After the midterm wins, Democrats will also wonder if a candidate could break through in North Carolina — or further. The party just won Senate seats in Texas, Alaska, South Carolina and Mississippi.

Ossoff is seen as a candidate willing to fight aggressively against President Trump and Republicans but not in a way that turns off swing voters.

Perhaps more than anyone else in the field, he is getting the ultimate compliment from Democrats: He is Obama-like.

“Ossoff has that [former President] Obama magic,” said John Morgan, the Democratic megadonor and prominent personal injury lawyer. “The ‘it’ factor.”

The biggest obstacle at this point is Ossoff himself. He has pledged that he would serve his full term, even as he is being prodded by Democrats to enter the race.

It’s not entirely clear he wants to run for president.

But if he does, many think he could win, which is why he tops this list for now.

While he wasn’t on the ballot, Newsom had reason to celebrate coming out of the midterms.

He emerged with political momentum following his redistricting efforts in California, which helped the party sweep to a huge majority in the House.

In the last year, as Republicans sought to redraw congressional maps, Newsom did the same in his state, proving to Democrats that he would take action to combat GOP efforts.

This week, he was also given what some allies say was a political gift of sorts, after Trump issued a public rebuke of the California Democrat’s commutation of death row inmates.

Trump basically picked a fight with Newsom, which put the governor squarely in the spotlight at a time when 2028 Democrats are trying to break through the noise.

It also might help Newsom appeal to primary voters.

More than most of the candidates, Newsom has already assembled much of the political infrastructure needed to launch a presidential bid. His small-dollar fundraising operation, powered by a list in the tens of millions, would give him a built-in way to raise money and organize right out of the gate.

And while his time is running down in the governor’s mansion, he spent the fall campaigning in states he will need to win in the early months of the primary season, building relationships with key state Democratic parties and their leaders.

The New York congresswoman is inarguably one of the biggest names in politics, and she brings with her an intensely loyal following, particularly among progressives.

She’s been wise with endorsements, backing Democratic Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and giving him a big donation. Last year, she backed New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) in his insurgent campaign.

Like Ossoff, there are questions about what Ocasio-Cortez, 37, will do next.

Will she run for the White House? Or will she run for a Senate seat in New York? What’s the best place for her?

Forecasts on how she would do also differ. Some say she could easily win a Democratic primary.

“If she decides to run, she could be unstoppable in a primary,” one Democratic strategist predicted.

Others wonder if Democratic primary voters will actually turn in 2028 to a progressive figure.

And despite the successes for the party in 2026, many Democrats are also unsure about nominating a woman in 2028 after the losses Hillary Clinton and former Vice President Kamala Harris suffered to Trump.

In the days following the midterms, moderate Democrats sought to make the case that Beshear’s star was rising.

They pointed to his tenure as chair of the Democratic Governors Association, which notched a series of wins in gubernatorial races this cycle including in Iowa and Texas.

Beshear also has an argument in a presidential primary: He has not only won twice in deep-red Kentucky, but he has maintained a high approval rating the entire time, appealing to the kinds of voters the party needs to win in 2028.

Some Democrats say his brand of politics — including his “nice guy” persona — is what the electorate will want following a divisive and contentious Trump era.

But he has the opposite problem Ocasio-Cortez faces.

While some say he could win in a general election, could he make it out of a Democratic primary, particularly as progressives have become the loudest voices inside the party?

“His candidacy will shine a light on where exactly the party is,” a second Democratic strategist said, adding, “It’s too soon to say.”

The former Transportation secretary comes into the 2028 cycle with a better resume than the one he had when he ran for president in 2020.

For starters, the former small-town mayor now has Cabinet-level experience, a large fundraising network and name recognition.

Buttigieg has also spent the last year weaving his way throughout the country to stump for midterm candidates, particularly in states he would need to win a primary, including South Carolina.

Buttigieg, who is one of the party’s best communicators, has also tried to make some inroads with Black voters. More than other potential candidates, he easily swept through both blue and purple districts, showing that he can appeal to a wide swath of voters.

But some wonder how he would stack up against potential center-left rivals such as Ossoff and Newsom.

“They would share that lane,” the second Democratic strategist said. “And I’m not sure how he’d differentiate himself in a crowded field. He’s gotta be thinking through all of that during the holidays.”

articles.title: Trump country cracked: 5 races that saw double-digit Trump territory fall to Democrats in 2026
articles.summary: Donald Trump carried Mississippi by nearly 23 points, yet Scott Colom beat Cindy Hyde-Smith by less than one, ending a 44-year GOP Senate drought.
articles.body: Donald Trump carried Mississippi by nearly 23 points in 2024. Two years later, Democrat Scott Colom won the state’s Senate race, ending a Republican hold that had lasted more than four decades. Colom’s victory was part of a string of Democratic breakthroughs during the midterms in places Trump had carried by double digits. Democrats also won Senate races in Kansas and South Carolina, captured the Texas governor’s office and flipped a Republican-held House seat deep in Trump country in Indiana that had not elected a Democrat since 1990. The results stand out for more than the presidential margins as well — Democrats broke Senate streaks that had lasted decades and defeated Republican incumbents in races many expected the GOP to hold, including one where the Democratic challenger spent next to nothing on television advertisements. FOX NEWS VOTER POLL: HOW DEMOCRATS TOOK CONTROL OF THE SENATE Here are five of the year’s most striking upsets: Scott Colom breaks Mississippi Democrats' 44-year Senate drought Trump carried the state by nearly 23 points in 2024, and a Democrat had not won a U.S. Senate race in Mississippi since 1982. Several major election forecasters rated the contest Solid Republican for much of the cycle, before shifting it to Likely Republican as the race tightened. Colom, a district attorney, defeated Republican incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, R-Miss., by less than one percentage point, 49.36% to 48.54%, according to Associated Press election results. Hyde-Smith had Trump’s backing, and the president rallied for her in the campaign’s final days. Meanwhile, the Senate Leadership Fund, a super PAC aligned with Senate GOP leadership, made a seven-figure late-campaign ad buy, as previously reported by Fox News Digital. The Associated Press did not call the race until Nov. 11, more than a week after Election Day. Colom will also become the first Black senator to represent Mississippi since Reconstruction. The margin was razor-thin, but the political barrier was enormous — a Trump +23 state, a Trump-backed incumbent and a 44-year drought in Democratic Senate victories. But Democrats pulled off the upset. Gina Hinojosa ends Texas' 36-year Democratic losing streak Hinojosa, a Democratic state representative, defeated three-term Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, R-Texas, as he sought an unprecedented fourth term, ending a 36-year Democratic losing streak in Texas governor’s races. Trump had carried the state by 13.7 points in 2024, according to Associated Press election data, and an October Fox News poll showed Abbott ahead leading up to the Nov. 3 election. Hinojosa, however, ultimately won with 52.8% of the vote to Abbott’s 45.7%, according to Associated Press election results. Her victory was a major break from Texas’ recent political history and a miss by many major polls. It also made Hinojosa the state’s first Latina governor. Democrats had not won the governor’s office since Ann Richards’ 1990 victory. Hinojosa’s win was one of two Democratic statewide breakthroughs in Texas, as Democratic state Rep. James Talarico also defeated Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton in the Senate race. CHUCK DEVORE: TEXAS TURNS BLUE, BUT HERE’S WHERE THE NEXT 4 BIG BATTLES ARE COMING Annie Andrews breaks through in South Carolina South Carolina had not elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1998, when Fritz Hollings won his final term, and Trump carried the state by nearly 18 points in 2024, according to Associated Press election data. Andrews, a Democratic pediatrician who had never held elected office before, defeated appointed Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, by nearly five points. Graham had Trump’s endorsement and the president also helped her with late campaign appearances on the trail. She had been appointed to serve out her brother’s term after his death, then won the Republican nomination for a full six-year term. Andrews’ win broke a nearly three-decade Republican hold on the state’s Senate seat and became a rare moment when a Trump-backed candidate lost in a state Republicans had long counted on. Adam Hamilton ends Kansas’ 94-year streak Kansas had not sent a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1932, when George McGill won a full term. Hamilton, a Democrat and the founding pastor of a large United Methodist church, defeated first-term Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., in a state Trump carried by 16 points in 2024, according to election data from the Associated Press. The Kansas race was long viewed as a Republican hold, but major election forecasters moved it into toss-up territory late in the campaign as Marshall faced scrutiny over his residency and lawsuits his former medical practice filed against patients. Trump and Vice President JD Vance both campaigned for Marshall, and Republican-aligned groups spent heavily to keep the seat, including more than $26 million committed to ads supporting him after the August primary — more than was spent on Marshall during his first race in 2020, according to AdImpact data cited by the Associated Press. Hamilton’s win ended a 94-year Republican Senate streak. J.D. Ford flips a longtime GOP district Democrat J.D. Ford defeated three-term Rep. Victoria Spartz, R-Ind., in Indiana’s 5th Congressional District, which Trump carried by about 17 points, according to Associated Press election results from 2024. Spartz had won re-election there by 18.6 points in 2024, and the district had not elected a Democrat since 1990, when Jim Jontz won. Ford, a Democratic state senator, won 51.7% to Spartz’s 48.3%, according to the Associated Press results after the midterms. His victory was the only Indiana House seat to change parties, making it a sharp reversal in a state that Trump carried by 19 points statewide in 2024. Democrat Richard Ojeda defeated Rep. Richard Hudson, R-N.C., who chaired the National Republican Congressional Committee, the House GOP’s campaign and fundraising arm. Hudson was charged with helping protect the Republican majority, and he had raised $4.2 million to Ojeda’s $2.9 million and won the district by nearly 19 points in 2024, while Trump had carried it by 16 points. articles.title: Debate a cuatro de las elecciones generales: horario, formato y dónde ver hoy por TV el cara a cara entre Abascal, Pedro Sánchez, Feijóo y Ada Colau
articles.standfirst: La cita de esta noche supone el último gran escaparate televisivo para movilizar al electorado indeciso
articles.summary: La cita de esta noche supone el último gran escaparate televisivo para movilizar al electorado indeciso
articles.body: La campaña de las elecciones generales encara su recta final este jueves 26 de noviembre a partir de las 22:00 horas con la celebración del debate a cuatro organizado por la Academia de Televisión. A apenas tres días de la apertura de las urnas este domingo 29 de noviembre, los candidatos de las cuatro principales formaciones nacionales —Pedro Sánchez (PSOE), Alberto Núñez Feijóo (PP), Santiago Abascal (Vox) y Ada Colau (Frente Amplio)— se reúnen por primera vez ante las cámaras en un encuentro moderado por la presidenta de la institución, María Casado. Tras el intenso cara a cara protagonizado la semana pasada por Sánchez y Feijóo y el posterior debate de portavoces en RTVE, la cita de esta noche supone el último gran escaparate televisivo para movilizar al electorado indeciso y fijar la política de alianzas tras el 29-N. La Junta Electoral Central desestimó finalmente el recurso de Podemos para incorporar a Irene Montero, confirmando así el formato a cuatro. El debate tendrá una duración aproximada de dos horas (hasta la medianoche) y se desarrollará de pie tras los atriles. Tras una ronda inicial de un minuto y medio por candidato para valorar la legislatura —que abrirá Ada Colau—, la confrontación se estructurará en cinco bloques temáticos de 20 minutos (con cinco minutos de intervención repartidos para cada aspirante): Como cierre, cada candidato dispondrá de un «minuto de oro» final para pedir directamente el voto a los ciudadanos, un turno que cerrará el líder del Partido Popular, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, según el orden establecido por sorteo. La señal institucional producida por la Academia de Televisión se emitirá de forma simultánea y gratuita en La 1, Canal 24 horas, Antena 3, laSexta, Telecinco, Cuatro, La Séptima, las cadenas autonómicas de la FORTA, RNE y en streaming a través de RTVE Play.

articles.title: Xi and Putin are thankful this year for Trump
articles.summary: Elevating Putin at his weakest is self-defeating, especially if Trump is serious about putting an end to Moscow’s war against Ukraine.
articles.body:
On Tuesday at the White House, President Trump pardoned two West Virginia-raised turkeys named Freedom and Feathers. Given his post-midterms pivot to China and Russia, it was hard not to see them as symbolic stand-ins for Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Since watching the country reject Trump’s second act in sweeping numbers — come January 3, 2027, Democrats will control the House and Senate — the cornered president has been on a global tour looking for redemption in low places.

His first attempt was in Shenzhen. During the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, Trump tried to boost his image by casting himself, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin as the modern-day equivalents of Franklin Roosevelt, Winston Churchill, and Joseph Stalin at Yalta.

It seemed lost on Trump that the balance of power has shifted since the end of World War II. In 1945, it was the U.S. and the United Kingdom keeping the Soviet Union in check. In 2026, it is China and Russia staring down the U.S.

Not that he noticed. It was clear that Xi’s decision to greet Trump at the airport — the first time the Chinese president has done that — was more than just reciprocating the U.S. president affording him that honor during his September State Visit.

Xi was effectively telling Trump, “You are in my multipolar world now.” It was also lost on Trump that Xi did the same thing for Putin.

Similar to Roosevelt humiliating Churchill at Yalta, Xi went out of his way to embarrass Putin during the summit. For starters, Trump and Xi arrived at the banquet together while Putin was forced to arrive separately.

Xi then thwarted Trump’s attempt to position Putin next to himself during the initial family summit photo. The Chinese president had choreographed the stage, and he was not going to let Trump upstage him. Finally, as if he was being relegated to the kids’ end of the Thanksgiving table, Putin was forced to sit to the left of Chinese First Lady Peng Liyuan, while Trump was afforded the place of honor to Xi’s right.

Beijing’s messaging was obvious. China is ascendant, the U.S. is staggering after being caught in Iran’s so-called ‘no war, no peace’ negotiating trap, and Russia is immolating its military and economy in Ukraine.

Xi seized the moment to loudly subordinate Russia to China on the global stage. Putin undoubtedly got the message. Nonetheless, he was cornered in Shenzhen until Trump took it upon himself to try to give him an out.

He posted a picture of him with Putin saying “My Friend.” Talk about looking for friends in low places. The Russian president is a wanted war criminal. On a daily basis, Putin intentionally targets, wounds, and kills Ukrainian civilians in a vain attempt to terrorize his way to a victory his military is unable to achieve.

Elevating Putin at his weakest is self-defeating, especially if Trump is serious about putting an end to Moscow’s war against Ukraine. It is also absurd given that Russia — like China — continues to provide the Islamic Republic of Iran with intel, arms, and dual-use technology in its war against the U.S.

Therein lies the rub. Trump, like an ailing Roosevelt at Yalta (who would die 60 days later), is blindly blundering his way into a new potentially existential Cold War wherein China and Russia would have the upper hand.

We see why. Trump, alongside Under Secretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby, are convinced that Washington can peel Putin away from Xi. But that is not going to happen. Beijing and Moscow are natural totalitarian allies and there is no geostrategic world wherein Russia sides with the U.S. against China.

Trump and Colby have repeatedly failed to grasp that. Instead, they are continuing to undermine NATO. They have now outrageously agreed to discuss Europe’s future security architecture with Putin as part of Russia-Ukraine peace talks.

But the talks won’t work, because Putin’s overarching goal is not peace. Rather, it is the complete destruction of NATO from within as a transatlantic defensive alliance.

The average American sees it. Eighty-one percent of registered voters viewed Putin and Russia unfavorably in October. Sixty-seven percent of Americans disapproved of Trump’s handling of Russia in a Pew poll that was released last week.

Yet Trump and Colby’s calculus remains muddled. Meanwhile, Xi sees a clearer path to seizing control of Taiwan one way or the other — and a down, but hardly out, Russia might be a month away from putting nukes in space .

The U.S. is never going to find allies in low places. Doing so makes us less secure, not more. It is time Trump and Colby understood that. China and Russia are not friends; they are ideological enemies — and sadly this Thanksgiving they are giving thanks for Trump’s evergreen strategic naïvete.

Mark Toth writes on national security and foreign policy. Col. (Ret.) Jonathan Sweet served 30 years as a military intelligence officer and led the U.S. European Command Intelligence Engagement Division from 2012 to 2014. They are the co-founders of INTREP360 and the INTREP360 Intelligence Report on Substack.

articles.title: A look at how the Trumps spend their Thanksgiving holiday through the years
articles.summary: Donald Trump marks his sixth Thanksgiving as president with the White House turkey pardon, after past holidays at Mar-a-Lago and Bagram Airfield.
articles.body: In keeping with tradition, President Donald Trump marked his sixth Thanksgiving in the executive office with the White House’s annual Turkey Pardon ceremony on Tuesday. His plans for Thanksgiving Day this year remain unannounced — but previous holidays offer a preview of how the president likes to spend the day honoring those who can't be at home for the uniquely American holiday due to service to the country. Last year, Trump spent Thanksgiving at Mar-a-Lago participating in his favorite pastime — golf. But he also used the time in what is known as the "Winter White House" to call Maj. Gen. Dave Gardner, commander of the 101st Airborne Division and Joint Task Force–Southern Border, by video conference and talk with troops deployed along the southern border. TRUMP AND DANA WHITE HONOR MARINE CORPS BAND WITH SIX-FIGURE CHECKS IN FIRST EVENT ON NEW HELIPAD First lady Melania Trump spent the days ahead of the holiday in 2025 visiting Camp Lejeune and Marine Corps Air Station New River with second lady Usha Vance on Nov. 19. They met with military families and made Thanksgiving crafts with children. In 2020, during the final Thanksgiving of his first term, Trump remained at the White House and made calls to six deployed military units representing every branch of the armed forces, including troops in Kuwait and sailors aboard the USS Winston Churchill in the Red Sea. Trump famously took a secret trip to Bagram Airfield in Afghanistan on Nov. 28, 2019, where he served turkey, posed for photos and thanked American troops for their sacrifices amid the ongoing war in the Middle East, which not even two years later, in August 2021, was brought to an end by then-President Joe Biden. "There's nowhere I'd rather celebrate this Thanksgiving than right here with the toughest, strongest, best, and bravest warriors on the face of the Earth," Trump told the troops at the time. "And you don't even know how much the people of our country love and respect you." TRUMP SAYS US MAY RECOVER ALL THE EQUIPMENT LEFT BEHIND IN AFGHANISTAN BY BIDEN ADMIN The visit came as roughly 12,000 American troops remained in Afghanistan more than 18 years after the U.S. invasion. During the visit, Trump met with Afghan President Ashraf Ghani to discuss efforts to end the war and told American troops that the Taliban wanted to reach a deal with the United States. He said his administration was reducing America's military presence in Afghanistan while pursuing a political solution to the more than 18-year conflict. Trump spent Thanksgiving 2018 in Florida having a traditional dinner with his family, including Melania and his children and grandchildren. He also held a video call with deployed troops before visiting Coast Guard members at Station Lake Worth Inlet with his wife, where the first couple thanked them for their service and hurricane rescues. After that holiday in 2018, Melania and then-second lady Karen Pence assembled comfort kits for deployed troops at American Red Cross headquarters. articles.title: Trump, NATO chief push Russia to avoid any actions that would 'expand the war' with Ukraine
articles.summary: President Donald Trump and NATO chief Mark Rutte, who met Wednesday night at Mar-a-Lago, urged Russia to avoid actions that might expand the Ukraine war.
articles.body: President Donald Trump and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte are calling on Russia to avoid making any moves "that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the war" against Ukraine. The declaration came after the pair got together at Trump's Mar-a-Lago residence in Florida on Thanksgiving Eve for what was described as an "outstanding meeting." However, Russia hit Kyiv with ballistic missiles overnight, according to the mayor of the Ukrainian capital. "The meeting was very impactful, with the war between Russia and Ukraine and the conflict in Iran being the primary subjects, as well as all of the record setting achievements that we have made together at the summits in the Hague and at Ankara," Trump and Rutte said in a joint statement. "We also discussed the importance of Russia avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the war, and the importance of obtaining a peaceful resolution to the war as rapidly as possible," the statement added. "Lastly, we talked about the importance of continuing to expand defense spending and investment in our industrial base, both in the United States and across NATO." PUTIN'S WAR DEATH TOLL REPORTEDLY TOPS 700,000 AS RUSSIA SCRAMBLES FOR RECRUITS Rutte said in a post on X following the meeting, "It’s clearer than ever that American leadership remains essential as we build a stronger Europe in a stronger NATO." The Kremlin on Thursday accused Ukraine of trying to expand the war after Ukraine sank a Russian warship in Libya using drones and attacked a Russian military-linked cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland this past weekend, Reuters reported. "As regards the escalation of the conflict in Ukraine, this appears to refer to attempts by the Kyiv regime to expand the geographical scope of this conflict. We are witnessing terrorist activity by the Kyiv regime in the Mediterranean and the Baltic," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov was quoted as saying. NATO SECRETARY GENERAL MARK RUTTE WARNS ON UKRAINE WAR RISKS AHEAD OF TRUMP MEETING "This cannot fail to cause concern amongst coastal states, and most likely within the Alliance as a whole — the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. Of course, nobody would want the conflict to spread geographically, and these are potentially very dangerous actions on the part of the Kyiv regime," Peskov added, according to Reuters. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said at least seven people were wounded in Russian strikes overnight, hitting a shopping center and other buildings, Reuters also reported.
